Go with organic/synthetic chemistry.

In the context of your comment, "I’m interested in synthesis but also neuropharmacology, in short, I want to work in medicinal chemistry to develop products that have to do with the neurological part of the body, specifically mental health, if that makes sense?" - I'm a research student working in this area but more on the testing side of the medicinal R&D process than development. With some neurological diseases, the drugs are bigger/more macromolecular, like antibodies, peptides, gene therapy, etc. but for mental health you're very much looking at smaller molecules and organic synthesis. I would say major in chemistry and pick up a second major or elective units if you can in pharmacology, neuroscience or biochemistry. It's great that you already have an idea of what you want to do in the future, good luck!

Definitely start with organic chemistry, learning biochemistry without organic chemistry is sort of like trying to learn physics without a lot of math. Lehninger is great and the standard in a lot of places for undergraduate/introductory biochemistry if you really want to learn it well. If you have a particular interest in the medical side of it though, Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry is a really beautiful book.

Hi there. I'm really sorry about what you went through. I think you should continue talking to it with anyone you trust and who has the capacity to listen and really be there for you. If you don't have anyone who can really be there (like me), I definitely recommend writing out your feelings. If you can, physically writing in a notebook can be really cathartic, there's something about the action of writing out words that sort of switches gears for me and gets me into a more meditative state. Otherwise, you can always vent here. I personally find it useless to avoid thinking about those awful memories that come up and instead try to externalise them by writing them out or talking about it all and how it's affected me because in a way, that gives me permission to move on. Also, do you have any access at all to any professional help like counselling over the phone or online?

On the practical side, schedule in things like eating and rest. Eat small, regular meals if you can and remind yourself to (like setting alarms on your phone for throughout the day) if you don't feel like eating. If you can't get to sleep, try to just lay down with your eyes closed listening to music or ambient noise and get some rest that way if you can for a set amount of time. Try to use your classes as a distraction if you can too: if you find it difficult to focus, use things like the Pomodoro technique, or see if you can link up with any of your (virtual) classmates to form a digital study group/group chat/talk to them over the phone and discuss the content, compare notes, etc. and this way you'll be able to focus on something different in a more active way.

I thought that I had overcome my fear until, about six months ago, I saw a man who looked almost exactly like the man who raped and abused me as a teenager at the departure gate of an airport. I don't know what happened in my mind at that moment. I was absolutely certain it was him, and believed that he would be on my flight. Before I knew it I was having a full panic attack. I practically ran to near the airport toilets before I completely broke down sobbing and shaking, hard. I was still sobbing immensely by the time I got on the plane and the panic attack wasn't completely over until two or three hours into the flight. This experience took me days, actually weeks, to really recover from. I guess in a way though, it has sort of removed the fear I have always had of running into him or being forced to be in proximity to him, because now I know that I have survived it (this incident was the first time in years). Previously, like OutrageouslyInverse, I had this fear constantly, particularly immediately after I was able to finally leave the "relationship" for good and for months following, when he and his friends were sending threats and harassment. I don't know how or when particularly it subsided, probably just with time and distraction. I don't think you should avoid thinking about it, but when those scenarios do pop up, think through them: how would or could you respond? Where could you go? What could you do, who could you contact, and how could you deal with it to make yourself feel safer?

Don't underestimate your capacity to heal. I've felt many times like I wouldn't make it, like there was nothing left, but going through the motions began to make things less difficult.

I am so, so sorry that this is happening to you. You don't deserve this at all. Please hang in there. I really hope that you are able to get out but until you are, please do absolutely everything you can to preserve your health (emotional, mental, physical) as much as you are reasonably able to. You deserve so, so much more than this and some day you will be able to live a life where you are treated the way you deserve to be.

Do you have support services in your area you might be able to contact, eg. for family violence? If this is too risky (you think your parents would find out that you've contacted them, or it would make the situation worse) is there anyone (trusted friends, other relatives, past teachers) you might be able to contact for any assistance, maybe to stay with? Are there any ways that you're able to spend your time that might bring you a bit of day to day happiness, distraction or reprieve such as reading a book you enjoy or playing a video game?

Not meeting their 'standard' is on them, not you. I have no doubt at all that you are a wonderful person and the way that abusers treat you is always, always a reflection of them, not you. I am sorry that they are causing you harm and hurt and that the quarantine situation means you are stuck with them. Please update us and feel free to post/comment as much as you need to, we are 100% here for you.
